summary: Specifies new IPFIX Information Elements to fix issues with the existing ipv6ExtensionHeaders and tcpOptions elements, especially the ability to export any observed IPv6 extension headers or TCP options.

plainLanguage.summary: Network monitors report what they saw in packets. The old report forms could not list every extra header or option. These new forms can.

questions: how to export ipv6 extension headers in ipfix
subtitle: New IPFIX fields that let flow exporters report any IPv6 extension header or TCP option they see.

tldr.problem: The older IPFIX elements ipv6ExtensionHeaders and tcpOptions could only report a frozen set of IPv6 extension headers and TCP options with Kind 63 or lower, and said nothing about order, counts, limits or lengths.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9740 defines twelve new Information Elements (513 to 524) that use a 256-bit flags type to cover every extension header and every TCP option Kind, plus lists, counts and chain lengths, and it deprecates the two old elements.
tldr.outcome: Exporters can now report any observed IPv6 extension header or TCP option, including ones they do not understand, and the old elements are deprecated in favor of the new ones.

today: RFC 9740 is a Proposed Standard from March 2025 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It deprecates the ipv6ExtensionHeaders and tcpOptions IPFIX elements in favor of the new ones.

sections.title: Problems With the Old Elements
sections.content:
IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX, RFC 7011) lets a router or probe report summaries of traffic flows. Each piece of reported data is an Information Element (IE). Two older IEs, ipv6ExtensionHeaders (64) and tcpOptions (209), were defined in RFC 5102 and have several gaps.

The ipv6ExtensionHeaders IE does not cover the full range of IPv6 extension headers, so it cannot report headers such as the Host Identity Protocol (139) or Shim6 (140) or those for experimentation. It also does not say how to export the order or number of occurrences of a header, whether the values are complete or cut off by a hardware limit, or how to report the length of the headers.

The tcpOptions IE can only export TCP options with a Kind of 63 or less. It cannot report the Experiment Identifiers (ExIDs) carried in shared experimental options (Kind 253 or 254, RFC 6994). Both IEs also lack an efficient encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: The old checklists had boxes only for a few well-known stickers. If a parcel carried a new kind of sticker, there was nowhere to tick it.

sections.title: IEs for IPv6 Extension Headers
sections.content:
Section 3 defines seven new IEs, numbered 513 to 519. ipv6ExtensionHeaderType (513) holds the type of one extension header seen in at least one packet of the Flow. ipv6ExtensionHeaderCount (514) holds how many consecutive times the same header type occurs.

ipv6ExtensionHeadersFull (515) is a set of flags with one bit per extension header. A bit is 1 if any observed packet in the Flow had that header. Bit 0 is the least significant bit, so common headers need only a few octets. The bit for "No Next Header" is set whenever that value is encountered, even though it is not strictly an extension header.

ipv6ExtensionHeaderTypeCountList (516) is a subTemplateList of type and count pairs that keeps the order of headers. For example, a Hop-by-Hop Options header, a Destination Options header, a Fragment header and another Destination Options header yield separate entries, so the two Destination Options groups stay distinct. If an implementation sees an extension header it does not support, it MUST echo the exact observed code.

ipv6ExtensionHeadersLimit (517) is a boolean. When false, the exported information covers only up to a limit set by hardware or software, not all headers. ipv6ExtensionHeadersChainLength (518) reports in octets the summed length of a chain of extension headers, which may help find the cause of packet drops. ipv6ExtensionHeaderChainLengthList (519) pairs each observed chain with its length. Each chain in a Flow with varying chains MUST be exported separately.

The ipv6ExtensionHeadersFull IE MUST NOT be exported together with ipv6ExtensionHeaderTypeCountList, because their scopes overlap.
sections.plainLanguage: One form ticks which kinds of stickers were on parcels. Another form lists the stickers in order, with how many in a row. A third says whether the counter ran out of room, and a fourth says how long the stack of stickers was.

sections.title: IEs for TCP Options
sections.content:
Section 4 defines five IEs, numbered 520 to 524. tcpOptionsFull (520) is a 256-bit flags value with one bit per TCP option number: Kind 0 is the least significant bit and Kind 255 is the most significant. Any observed option can be reported, even one the exporter does not understand, and no mapping table needs updating.

Shared experimental options (Kind 253 or 254) are reported through ExIDs instead. tcpSharedOptionExID16 (521) carries a 2-byte ExID and tcpSharedOptionExID32 (522) carries a 4-byte ExID. Their list forms, tcpSharedOptionExID16List (523) and tcpSharedOptionExID32List (524), are basicLists of those values. When these list IEs are present, the exporter MUST NOT set the Kind 253 or 254 bits in tcpOptionsFull for the same Flow.

Implementations are assumed to have a list of valid ExIDs. Without it they cannot tell whether an ExID is present or whether it is 2 or 4 bytes long. If a Flow mixes 2-byte and 4-byte ExIDs, the same Template Record is used with both IEs.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one big tick-box sheet for every numbered TCP option. Special mystery options get their own name tags, which come in short and long sizes.

sections.title: Encoding and Examples
sections.content:
The flags IEs use a new abstract data type, unsigned256, a non-negative integer from 0 to 2^256 - 1 in network byte order. Reduced-size encoding (RFC 7011 Section 6.2) applies: leading zero octets are dropped, so a value that fits in one octet is sent as one octet.

The examples in Section 6 show this. A Flow that only had a Destination Options header (bit 0) sends 0x01. A Flow with Destination Options (0), Hop-by-Hop Options (1) and Routing (5) sends 0x23. A chain of Routing (5), Mobility (7) and Authentication (9) headers is 0x02A0. For TCP, a Flow with End of Option List (0), Maximum Segment Size (2) and Window Scale (3) sends 0x0D.

A further example shows a list of shared option ExIDs: 0x0348 (HOST_ID) and 0x454E (TCP-ENO) as 2-byte values, and 0xE2D4C3D9 (Shared Memory Communications over RDMA) as a 4-byte value.
sections.plainLanguage: If only the first few boxes are ticked, you do not need to send the whole huge sheet. You just send the short part that has any ticks, and skip the empty zeros.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA marked ipv6ExtensionHeaders (64) and tcpOptions (209) as deprecated in favor of ipv6ExtensionHeadersFull and tcpOptionsFull, and added the twelve new IEs (513 to 524) to the IPFIX registry. It also added unsigned256 as data type 23.

A new registry, "IPFIX ipv6ExtensionHeaders Bits", maps bit positions to extension headers. Initial bits are 0 DST (60), 1 HOP (0), 2 NoNxt (59), 3 UNK, 4 FRA0 (44, first fragment), 5 RH (43), 6 FRA1 (44, not first fragment), 7 MOB (135), 8 ESP (50), 9 AH (51), 10 HIP (139), 11 SHIM6 (140), and bits 12 and 13 for protocol numbers 253 and 254, which are for experimentation and testing. Bits 14 to 255 are unassigned.

When a new code is assigned in the IPv6 Extension Header Types registry, IANA picks the next free bit automatically. Other changes go through Expert Review.
sections.plainLanguage: The official catalog now says the old forms are retired and lists the new ones. A new numbered chart tells everyone which box means which sticker, and new stickers get the next empty box.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the IPFIX security considerations in Section 11 of RFC 7011. It adds one concern: the ipv6ExtensionHeadersChainLength and ipv6ExtensionHeadersLimit IEs could be used by an unauthorized observer to deduce the processing capabilities of nodes. Section 8 of RFC 7012 describes the measures needed to protect the integrity and confidentiality of exported information.

For the other IEs, the document says it adds no new security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger reads the reports, they might learn how much a router can handle. So the reports should be kept private and safe from tampering.

Flags for any IPv6 extension header
